notes: So, a decision model. You send it text and a typed question with your options, and you get back one of those options and a probability, in one pass. It can't invent a label and it can't explain itself. That's System One. The "wait, is this even the right question?" check is System Two, and you build that yourself.

notes: Typed output fixes the format, and the decision can still be wrong. These models mostly gave the same answer every time, so a wrong answer is the same wrong answer at scale, and nothing warns you. Miss that report, or publish the wrong testimonial, and the candidate tells X and Reddit how they were treated, it trends, and good luck with building your brilliant startup without being able to hire good people willing to work for you.

          On these 60 reviews, Jev's confidence tracked how often it was right: pooled over 720 answers the average gap was 0.011, while Clef Flash's was 0.358. And Jev called the cancelled-train review not a testimonial at 0.96, and the key says the opposite. On sentiment, a 0.9 cutoff threw away nine good answers to catch four bad ones. notes: The first fix I'd reach for is a longer prompt. In these saved runs, adding classifier framing scored higher in 15 of 39 setups, the same in 15, lower in 9, and adding the tree on top scored higher in 4, the same in 14, lower in 21. Cloudflare's Clef went 54, 51, 49 in every pass, though that route may only read the first 2,000 tokens of state. I voted Jev's three passes, and the majority never beat its best single pass. Fine-tuning starts paying off around 200 labels, and we've got 9 testimonials. And when two models are both wrong, they pick the same wrong answer 60% of the time, so the second opinion has to come from a different model.

            Q: Would agree-or-defer hold in production? A: Unknown. The rule was fixed before the pairs were computed but scored on the same 60 reviews used for everything else, and the human review cost of the deferred set is unmeasured. Treat it as a policy to test.
            Q: CTO: with your full policy, how big is the human queue? A: On this set, 35 of 60. Split it the way the workflow does: 25 reviews either model flagged as a serious concern go to a person, and on this set those flags covered all 25 reference concerns for every pair. Of the other 35 reviews the rule auto-accepts 25 and sends 10 to a person, 6 by disagreement and 4 by a "can't tell". The set is concern-heavy by design. On real feedback the share depends on how often concerns happen, which this can't tell you.

steps.text: classification-bench runs this test on your own cases, labels and questions. | Bring any model through an OpenRouter key, or Claude Code and Codex on the subscription you already have. | Bring data | your inputs, your labels | Plan | models, prompts, passes | Run | stays inside your budget | Evaluate | agreement, answer changes | Report | per label, per pass | OpenRouter | Cloudflare Clef | Claude Code | Codex | Liquid / Solar / Qwen

notes: So, this benchmark taught me what a runner has to do: count missing answers, reject broken formats, keep labels away from the model, know what each request cost, run it more than once. I pulled those lessons into a tool called classification-bench: your inputs, your labels, and it reports agreement and how often an answer flips between repeats. Where it stands: the pipeline runs offline with more than 400 tests, it has made small real calls through OpenRouter and Cloudflare's Clef, the Claude Code and Codex routes are built but untested live, and we're open-sourcing it, so ask me for early access.

Q: Jev found every serious concern but missed the testimonial. Why? A: It found all 25. Its three misses on that field were "can't tell" reviews it called no. notes:
Q: Why not pay for Opus at 59? A: You can, at about 38 times the estimated spend, and Opus held 58 to 59 over three passes against Jev's 52 to 54. Sonnet scored 58 in all nine cells and still changed two reviews between passes, so the aggregate hides movement on the hard ones.
            Q: Is 54 versus 59 real on 60 reviews? A: It held across three passes each: Jev 54, 53, 52 and Opus 59, 58, 58. On first passes Opus matched five reviews Jev missed and missed none Jev matched. It's still one set of 60 synthetic reviews and a provisional key, so read it as a direction.
            Q: Decision models don't hallucinate, so isn't the risk gone? A: A typed head can't invent a label, and on this set 31 of 50 decision-model groups gave identical answers across three passes, so one failure class is gone. The other stays: Perplexity Decider matched 54 of 60 in all nine runs with the same errors every time, so a wrong answer is the same wrong answer at scale, with no variance to warn you. Miss a harassment report or publish the wrong testimonial and the candidate tells X and Reddit how they were treated.
